claim: (R)-DI-87 is a clinical-stage anticancer drug and potent inhibitor of mammalian deoxycytidine kinase (dCK).
source: (R)-DI-87, a clinical-stage anticancer drug and potent inhibitor of mammalian deoxycytidine kinase (dCK), mitigates Staphylococcus aureus abscess formation in organ tissues upon invasive bloodstream infection.
evidence: Referenced as a clinical-stage anticancer drug with citation to Poddar et al., 2020

claim: (R)-DI-87 mitigates Staphylococcus aureus abscess formation in organ tissues upon invasive bloodstream infection.
source: (R)-DI-87, a clinical-stage anticancer drug and potent inhibitor of mammalian deoxycytidine kinase (dCK), mitigates Staphylococcus aureus abscess formation in organ tissues upon invasive bloodstream infection.
evidence: Primary finding stated in abstract and supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: (R)-DI-87 shields phagocytes from staphylococcal death-effector deoxyribonucleosides that target dCK and the mammalian purine salvage pathway-apoptosis axis.
source: Mechanistically, (R)-DI-87 shields phagocytes from staphylococcal death-effector deoxyribonucleosides that target dCK and the mammalian purine salvage pathway-apoptosis axis.
evidence: Mechanistic explanation supported by cytotoxicity assays and caspase-3 activity data in Figures 2 and 3

claim: (R)-DI-87-mediated protection of immune cells amplifies macrophage infiltration into deep-seated abscesses.
source: In this manner, (R)-DI-87-mediated protection of immune cells amplifies macrophage infiltration into deep-seated abscesses, a phenomenon coupled with enhanced pathogen control, ameliorated immunopathology, and reduced disease severity.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data showing F4/80-positive macrophages in Figure 5

claim: (R)-DI-87-mediated protection of immune cells is coupled with enhanced pathogen control, ameliorated immunopathology, and reduced disease severity.
source: In this manner, (R)-DI-87-mediated protection of immune cells amplifies macrophage infiltration into deep-seated abscesses, a phenomenon coupled with enhanced pathogen control, ameliorated immunopathology, and reduced disease severity.
evidence: Supported by bacterial burden data and histopathology in Figure 4

claim: Pharmaceutical blockade of dCK represents an advanced anti-infective intervention strategy against which staphylococci cannot develop resistance.
source: Thus, pharmaceutical blockade of dCK represents an advanced anti-infective intervention strategy against which staphylococci cannot develop resistance and may help to fight fatal infectious diseases in hospitalized patients.
evidence: Inference based on host-directed therapy concept that targets host factors rather than bacterial components

claim: Hospital- and community-acquired infections caused by antibiotic-resistant bacterial pathogens represent a global public health threat.
source: Hospital- and community-acquired infections caused by antibiotic-resistant bacterial pathogens represent a global public health threat (Wenzel, 2007; GBD 2019 Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators, 2022a; GBD 2019 Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators, 2022b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Infections caused by multidrug-resistant microbes are often associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as compared to infections caused by antibiotic-sensitive strains.
source: Specifically, infections caused by multidrug-resistant microbes are often associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as compared to infections caused by antibiotic-sensitive strains (Klevens et al., 2008; Yaw et al., 2014; GBD 2019 Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators, 2022a; GBD 2019 Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators, 2022b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: S. aureus colonizes approximately 30% of the human population.
source: Of particular concern are Mycobacteria, certain Gram-negative as well as Gram-positive bacteria including Staphylococcus aureus, a notorious pathogen that colonizes approximately 30% of the human population (Lowy, 1998; Kuehnert et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: S. aureus causes skin and soft tissue infections and is a widespread cause of endocarditis, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, bacteremia, and sepsis.
source: S. aureus causes skin and soft tissue infections and is a widespread cause of endocarditis, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, bacteremia, and sepsis (Lowy, 1998; Fridkin et al., 2005; Klevens et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: A hallmark of staphylococcal disease is the formation of suppurative abscesses.
source: Nonetheless, a hallmark of staphylococcal disease is the formation of suppurative abscesses, where S. aureus provokes inflammatory responses that attract neutrophils, macrophages, and other immune cells to the site of the infection (Lowy, 1998; Cheng et al., 2011; Spaan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: S. aureus rapidly evades NET-mediated killing due to the secretion of a potent nuclease (Nuc) capable of disrupting these structures.
source: However, S. aureus rapidly evades NET-mediated killing due to the secretion of a potent nuclease (Nuc) capable of disrupting these structures (Berends et al., 2010; von Köckritz-Blickwede and Winstel, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Nuc-mediated degradation of NETs leads to the release of deoxyribonucleoside monophosphates that can be converted by the staphylococcal cell surface protein AdsA into death-effector deoxyribonucleosides.
source: Intriguingly, Nuc-mediated degradation of NETs leads to the release of deoxyribonucleoside monophosphates that can be converted by the staphylococcal cell surface protein AdsA (adenosine synthase A) into death-effector deoxyribonucleosides (Thammavongsa et al., 2013; Tantawy et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: AdsA-derived death-effector deoxyribonucleosides such as deoxyadenosine (dAdo) and deoxyguanosine (dGuo) display toxigenic properties and contribute to immune cell death during acute and persistent S. aureus infections.
source: Notably, AdsA-derived death-effector deoxyribonucleosides such as deoxyadenosine (dAdo) and deoxyguanosine (dGuo) display toxigenic properties and contribute to immune cell death during acute and persistent S. aureus infections (Thammavongsa et al., 2013; Winstel et al., 2019; Tantawy et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: dAdo and dGuo-triggered phagocyte cell death involves the uptake of dAdo and dGuo via human equilibrative nucleoside transporter 1 (hENT1), intracellular phosphorylation of dAdo and dGuo by adenosine kinase (ADK) and deoxycytidine kinase (dCK), and subsequent imbalanced expansion of intracellular dATP and dGTP pools which trigger caspase-3-dependent immune cell death.
source: More precisely, dAdo and dGuo-triggered phagocyte cell death involves the uptake of dAdo and dGuo via human equilibrative nucleoside transporter 1 (hENT1), intracellular phosphorylation of dAdo and dGuo by adenosine kinase (ADK) and deoxycytidine kinase (dCK), and subsequent imbalanced expansion of intracellular dATP and dGTP pools which trigger caspase-3-dependent immune cell death (Winstel et al., 2018; Tantawy et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Genetic disruption of the metabolic cascade involving dCK rendered macrophages resistant to AdsA-derived death-effector deoxyribonucleosides, leading to the accumulation of phagocytes within the deeper cavity of abscesses and accelerated clearance of staphylococci in vivo.
source: Of note, genetic disruption of this metabolic cascade rendered macrophages resistant to AdsA-derived death-effector deoxyribonucleosides, leading to the accumulation of phagocytes within the deeper cavity of abscesses and accelerated clearance of staphylococci in vivo (Winstel et al., 2018; Winstel et al., 2019; Tantawy et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: (R)-DI-87-mediated inhibition of mammalian dCK in U937 or U937 MФ efficiently prevented dAdo- or dGuo-induced cell death in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Of note, (R)-DI-87-mediated inhibition of mammalian dCK in U937 or U937 MФ efficiently prevented dAdo- or dGuo-induced cell death in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2A–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-D

claim: Pre-treatment of primary human CD14+ monocytes or human monocyte-derived macrophages (HMDMs) with (R)-DI-87 blocked dAdo- or dGuo-triggered cytotoxicity.
source: In addition, we observed that pre-treatment of primary human CD14+ monocytes or human monocyte-derived macrophages (HMDMs) with (R)-DI-87 blocked dAdo- or dGuo-triggered cytotoxicity suggesting that dCK inhibition may suppress the toxigenic properties of staphylococcal death-effector deoxyribonucleosides (Figure 2E–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-H

claim: (R)-DI-87-exposed cells were fully protected against the cytotoxic effect of dAdo and dGuo produced by rAdsA.
source: While enzymatic reactions that contained rAdsA and purine deoxyribonucleoside monophosphates triggered cell death of human monocytes or macrophages in this approach, (R)-DI-87-exposed cells were fully protected against the cytotoxic effect of dAdo and dGuo further indicating that inhibition of mammalian dCK helps to neutralize AdsA-derived death-effector deoxyribonucleosides (Figure 2I–J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I-J

claim: Macrophage killing required purine deoxyribonucleoside monophosphate-conditioned media and adsA-proficient staphylococci as only wild-type S. aureus Newman and dAMP- or dGMP-supplemented media triggered phagocyte cell death.
source: In line with earlier studies (Thammavongsa et al., 2013; Winstel et al., 2018; Winstel et al., 2019; Tantawy et al., 2022), macrophage killing required purine deoxyribonucleoside monophosphate-conditioned media and adsA-proficient staphylococci as only wild-type S. aureus Newman and dAMP- or dGMP-supplemented media triggered phagocyte cell death in this approach (Figure 2K–L).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K-L and citations to published literature

claim: (R)-DI-87-exposed cells could not be killed by S. aureus- and AdsA-derived death-effector deoxyribonucleosides.
source: However, (R)-DI-87-exposed cells could not be killed in these experiments supporting the idea that pharmacological inhibition of host dCK can shield macrophages from S. aureus- and AdsA-driven cell death (Figure 2K–L).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K-L

claim: (R)-DI-87 is a suitable small molecule dCK inhibitor capable of preventing host immune cell death induced by toxigenic products of the staphylococcal Nuc/AdsA pathway.
source: Collectively, these initial data demonstrate that (R)-DI-87 is a suitable small molecule dCK inhibitor capable of preventing host immune cell death induced by toxigenic products of the staphylococcal Nuc/AdsA pathway.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on data presented in Figure 2

claim: (R)-DI-87-treatment of U937 or U937 MФ significantly decreased dAdo- or dGuo-mediated activation of caspase-3 activity.
source: As expected, (R)-DI-87-treatment of U937 or U937 MФ significantly decreased dAdo- or dGuo-mediated activation of caspase-3 activity (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-D

claim: (R)-DI-87-mediated dCK inhibition selectively prevented dAdo- or dGuo-mediated induction of apoptotic cell death in host immune cells.
source: Since caspase-3 represents the key modulator of the apoptosis signaling pathway, these data suggest that (R)-DI-87-mediated dCK inhibition selectively prevented dAdo- or dGuo-mediated induction of apoptotic cell death in host immune cells (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: Inference based on caspase-3 activity data shown in Figure 3A-D and established knowledge about caspase-3 function

claim: (R)-DI-87-treatment of U937 or U937 MФ prevented caspase-3 activation as detected by immunoblotting.
source: In agreement with the enzymatic activity assay, (R)-DI-87-treatment of U937 or U937 MФ prevented caspase-3 activation (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3E-F

claim: (R)-DI-87 inhibited activation of programmed cell death and apoptosis as positive signals for annexin-V/PI were strongly decreased in samples that have been exposed to the dCK inhibitor.
source: Microscopy-based analysis of (R)-DI-87- and death-effector deoxyribonucleoside-exposed macrophages confirmed that (R)-DI-87 inhibited activation of programmed cell death and apoptosis as positive signals for annexin-V/PI were strongly decreased in samples that have been exposed to the dCK inhibitor (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3G-H

claim: Administration of (R)-DI-87 and associated inhibition of mammalian dCK prevents apoptotic cell death in phagocytes caused by S. aureus AdsA-derived death-effector deoxyribonucleosides.
source: Together, these data indicate that administration of (R)-DI-87 and associated inhibition of mammalian dCK prevents apoptotic cell death in phagocytes caused by S. aureus AdsA-derived death-effector deoxyribonucleosides.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on data presented in Figure 3

claim: Continuous treatment of animals with (R)-DI-87 did not alter the immune cell composition of peripheral blood.
source: Continuous treatment of animals with (R)-DI-87 did not alter the immune cell composition of peripheral blood (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by FACS-based immuno-phenotyping data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Endpoint analysis uncovered no developmental errors or differences in lymphocyte development as immune cell profiles of spleen tissues along with organ cellularity or mouse body weights were unaffected by (R)-DI-87 treatment.
source: Likewise, endpoint analysis (day 23) uncovered no developmental errors or differences in lymphocyte development as immune cell profiles of spleen tissues along with organ cellularity or mouse body weights were unaffected by (R)-DI-87 treatment (Figure 4B–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B-D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Administration of (R)-DI-87 to mice did not cause any other obvious phenotype during this procedure but led to the accumulation of deoxycytidine, the natural substrate of dCK, in plasma.
source: Further, administration of (R)-DI-87 to mice did not cause any other obvious phenotype during this procedure but led to the accumulation of deoxycytidine, the natural substrate of dCK (Reichard, 1988; Arnér and Eriksson, 1995), in plasma suggesting that (R)-DI-87 not only represents a safe but also highly selective inhibitor of host dCK (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS-MRM analysis data shown in Figure 4E and citations to published literature

claim: Abscess numbers and bacterial loads were significantly reduced in livers and kidneys in (R)-DI-87-treated animals as compared to control mice.
source: Notably, abscess numbers and bacterial loads were significantly reduced in livers and kidneys in (R)-DI-87-treated animals as compared to control mice validating (R)-DI-87 as a novel host-directed and anti-infective drug that protects against staphylococcal abscess formation (Figure 4F–I).
evidence: Supported by bacterial burden and abscess enumeration data shown in Figure 4F-I

claim: (R)-DI-87-treated animals no longer displayed increased resistance to S. aureus infection when challenged with the S. aureus Newman adsA mutant.
source: To test whether S. aureus exploits the activity of dCK along with the purine salvage pathway during infection, cohorts of mice were also challenged with the S. aureus Newman adsA mutant. (R)-DI-87-treated animals no longer displayed increased resistance to S. aureus infection (Figure 4F–I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4F-I

claim: Infection with S. aureus adsA-deficient bacteria phenocopied (R)-DI-87-mediated inhibition of dCK.
source: Moreover, infection with S. aureus adsA-deficient bacteria phenocopied (R)-DI-87-mediated inhibition of dCK, in line with the concept that AdsA is required for establishing persistent infections in host tissues (Figure 4F–I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4F-I

claim: Histopathological analysis of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained liver or renal tissues revealed that wild-type S. aureus Newman formed structured abscesses in vehicle-treated mice.
source: As expected, histopathological analysis of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained liver or renal tissues revealed that wild-type S. aureus Newman formed structured abscesses in vehicle-treated mice (Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by histopathology images shown in Figure 4J

claim: Lesions obtained from (R)-DI-87-treated animals appeared smaller in size and typically did not harbor a discernable organization of staphylococci.
source: However, lesions obtained from (R)-DI-87-treated animals appeared smaller in size and typically did not harbor a discernable organization of staphylococci, further demonstrating that administration of (R)-DI-87 represents a medically valuable strategy to mitigate S. aureus abscess formation (Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by histopathology images shown in Figure 4J

claim: (R)-DI-87 neither improved the killing of S. aureus in human or mouse blood, nor it displayed antimicrobial activity.
source: Presumably, (R)-DI-87-treatment protects macrophages against AdsA-derived death-effector deoxyribonucleosides and therefore enhances phagocyte survival during abscess formation as (R)-DI-87 neither improved the killing of S. aureus in human or mouse blood, nor it displayed antimicrobial activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B and Supplementary file 1

claim: Inhibition of mammalian dCK by (R)-DI-87 attenuates S. aureus abscess formation and disease pathogenesis in vivo.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that inhibition of mammalian dCK by (R)-DI-87 attenuates S. aureus abscess formation and disease pathogenesis in vivo.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on data presented in Figure 4

claim: Immunofluorescence staining of tissue abscesses obtained from vehicle-treated animals revealed that F4/80-positive macrophages resided at the periphery of infectious foci.
source: As expected, immunofluorescence staining of tissue abscesses obtained from vehicle-treated animals revealed that F4/80-positive macrophages resided at the periphery of infectious foci (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5A-D

claim: Lesions derived from mice that received (R)-DI-87 contained infiltrates of F4/80-positive macrophages within the neutrophil cuff.
source: On the contrary, lesions derived from mice that received (R)-DI-87 differed as they contained infiltrates of F4/80-positive macrophages within the neutrophil cuff, suggesting that (R)-DI-87-mediated inhibition of host dCK terminates macrophage exclusion from staphylococcal infectious foci (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5E-H

claim: adsA mutant-derived tissue lesions were characterized by increased infiltration rates of F4/80-positive phagocytes, irrespectively of whether animals were treated with (R)-DI-87 or vehicle during the course of the infection.
source: Of note, adsA mutant-derived tissue lesions were also characterized by increased infiltration rates of F4/80-positive phagocytes, irrespectively of whether animals were treated with (R)-DI-87 or vehicle during the course of the infection (Figure 5I–P).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5I-P

claim: (R)-DI-87-mediated blockade of host dCK phenocopied the adsA mutation in S. aureus.
source: Thus, (R)-DI-87-mediated blockade of host dCK phenocopied the adsA mutation in S. aureus.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of data from (R)-DI-87-treated and adsA mutant-infected mice

claim: BMDMs exposed to (R)-DI-87 displayed increased resistance toward dAdo and dGuo compared to vehicle-treated cells.
source: Compared to vehicle-treated cells, which were susceptible to death-effector deoxyribonucleosides, BMDMs exposed to (R)-DI-87 displayed increased resistance toward dAdo and dGuo presumably explaining their abundance in infectious foci obtained from wild-type S. aureus Newman-challenged and dCK inhibitor-treated mice (Figure 5Q–R).
evidence: Supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 5Q-R

claim: Sex might not impact the efficacy of (R)-DI-87 in laboratory animals.
source: Similar findings were also obtained for male animal-derived BMDMs suggesting that sex might not impact the efficacy of (R)-DI-87 in laboratory animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B

claim: (R)-DI-87-treatment protects macrophages from staphylococcal death-effector deoxyribonucleosides and therefore boosts their infiltration into persistent abscesses in organ tissues.
source: In summary, these data suggest that (R)-DI-87-treatment protects macrophages from staphylococcal death-effector deoxyribonucleosides and therefore boosts their infiltration into persistent abscesses in organ tissues (Figure 6).
evidence: Summary conclusion based on data presented in Figure 5 and illustrated in Figure 6

claim: Host-directed therapy (HDT) targets host-encoded factors required for pathogen replication and survival without interfering with microbial growth or metabolism, thereby eliminating the risk of resistance development.
source: Specifically, HDT targets host-encoded factors required for pathogen replication and survival without interfering with microbial growth or metabolism, thereby eliminating the risk of resistance development.
evidence: Definition of HDT concept based on established knowledge

claim: Many clinically relevant pathogens have already developed resistance-mechanisms against many last-resort antibiotics thereby rendering antibiotic therapy of appropriate infections often ineffective.
source: However, many clinically relevant pathogens have already developed resistance-mechanisms against many of these drugs thereby rendering antibiotic therapy of appropriate infections often ineffective (Meka and Gold, 2004; Chambers and Deleo, 2009; GBD 2019 Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators, 2022a; GBD 2019 Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators, 2022a).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The rapid exchange of antibiotic resistance genes via horizontal gene transfer events, along with the large-scale usage of antimicrobials in hospitals and in the animal industry, continuously triggers the emergence of new drug-resistant and globally spreading bacterial clones.
source: Moreover, the rapid exchange of antibiotic resistance genes via horizontal gene transfer events, along with the large-scale usage of antimicrobials in hospitals and in the animal industry, continuously triggers the emergence of new drug-resistant and globally spreading bacterial clones, highlighting the desperate need for novel treatment options to fight infectious diseases in human or animal hosts (Chambers and Deleo, 2009; Nübel, 2016; Jian et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: S. aureus triggers toxic shock syndrome, food poisoning, ventilator-associated pneumonia, and associated infections of the respiratory tract.
source: Moreover, this microbe triggers toxic shock syndrome, food poisoning, ventilator-associated pneumonia, and associated infections of the respiratory tract (Lowy, 1998; Lee et al., 2018; Torres et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Abscess formation is accompanied by liquefaction necrosis, the release of purulent exudates into circulating body fluids, and several defensive host responses designed to limit staphylococcal replication and spread.
source: Abscess formation is further accompanied by liquefaction necrosis, the release of purulent exudates into circulating body fluids, and several defensive host responses designed to limit staphylococcal replication and spread (Cheng et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Staphylococcal invasion of host tissues and abscess formation includes deposition of structural fibrin clusters, which shield healthy tissues from disseminating staphylococci.
source: For example, staphylococcal invasion of host tissues and abscess formation includes deposition of structural fibrin clusters, which shield healthy tissues from disseminating staphylococci (Cheng et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Neutrophils combat S. aureus by powerful mechanisms which involve phagocytosis, generation of reactive oxygen species, and the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs).
source: Moreover, neutrophils combat S. aureus by powerful mechanisms which involve phagocytosis, generation of reactive oxygen species, and the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) (Spaan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: NETs represent an extracellular matrix composed of nuclear and mitochondrial DNA spiked with antimicrobial peptides, cell-specific proteases, and granular proteins that together ensnare and kill microbial invaders.
source: NETs represent an extracellular matrix composed of nuclear and mitochondrial DNA spiked with antimicrobial peptides, cell-specific proteases, and granular proteins that together ensnare and kill microbial invaders (Brinkmann et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: dCK is a rate-limiting enzyme of the nucleoside salvage pathway that catalyzes the intracellular conversion of deoxyribonucleosides into deoxyribonucleoside monophosphates.
source: Since dCK is a rate-limiting enzyme of the nucleoside salvage pathway that catalyzes the intracellular conversion of deoxyribonucleosides into deoxyribonucleoside monophosphates (Arnér and Eriksson, 1995), (R)-DI-87-mediated inhibition of dCK most likely suppresses an uncontrolled biogenesis of deoxyribonucleoside di- and triphosphates that may trigger replication errors and apoptosis in host cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: (R)-DI-87-mediated inhibition of dCK most likely suppresses an uncontrolled biogenesis of deoxyribonucleoside di- and triphosphates that may trigger replication errors and apoptosis in host cells.
source: Since dCK is a rate-limiting enzyme of the nucleoside salvage pathway that catalyzes the intracellular conversion of deoxyribonucleosides into deoxyribonucleoside monophosphates (Arnér and Eriksson, 1995), (R)-DI-87-mediated inhibition of dCK most likely suppresses an uncontrolled biogenesis of deoxyribonucleoside di- and triphosphates that may trigger replication errors and apoptosis in host cells.
evidence: Inference based on known function of dCK and mechanism of (R)-DI-87

claim: dCK deficiency in phagocytes or other cells such as lymphoblasts prevents an overload of intracellular deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates upon exposure to death-effector deoxyribonucleosides.
source: Consistent with this model, earlier work suggested that dCK deficiency in phagocytes or other cells such as lymphoblasts prevents an overload of intracellular deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates upon exposure to death-effector deoxyribonucleosides (Gudas et al., 1978; Winstel et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Inhibition of host dCK represents an attractive host-directed therapeutic intervention strategy that terminates a refined immuno-evasive maneuver S. aureus has evolved to establish persistent infections in mammalian hosts.
source: Thus, inhibition of host dCK represents an attractive host-directed therapeutic intervention strategy that terminates a refined immuno-evasive maneuver S. aureus has evolved to establish persistent infections in mammalian hosts.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data and mechanistic understanding

claim: (R)-DI-87 does not exhibit detrimental side effects as (R)-DI-87-exposed laboratory animals neither lost weight during long-term treatment nor displayed any other adverse effects that may negatively affect host immune responses.
source: In particular, (R)-DI-87 does not exhibit detrimental side effects as (R)-DI-87-exposed laboratory animals neither lost weight during long-term treatment nor displayed any other adverse effects that may negatively affect host immune responses.
evidence: Supported by safety assessment data in Figure 4A-D

claim: The immune cell composition profile of mice that received (R)-DI-87 was not altered when compared to mice that received the vehicle control.
source: Specifically, the immune cell composition profile of mice that received (R)-DI-87 was not altered when compared to mice that received the vehicle control.
evidence: Supported by FACS-based immuno-phenotyping data in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Patrolling neutrophils known to play a significant role during staphylococcal infections along with other crucial elements of the host immune system are fully functional in (R)-DI-87-treated hosts.
source: This suggests that patrolling neutrophils known to play a significant role during staphylococcal infections (Spaan et al., 2013) along with other crucial elements of the host immune system are fully functional in (R)-DI-87-treated hosts, thereby offering tremendous opportunities to improve infection outcomes in hospitalized or critically ill patients.
evidence: Inference based on immune cell profiling data and citation to published literature

claim: Usage of (R)-DI-87 represents a host-directed and anti-infective therapeutic approach to which S. aureus and other multidrug-resistant bacteria cannot develop resistance mechanisms.
source: Further, usage of (R)-DI-87 represents a host-directed and anti-infective therapeutic approach to which S. aureus and other multidrug-resistant bacteria cannot develop resistance mechanisms.
evidence: Inference based on host-directed therapy concept

claim: Many other medically highly relevant bacterial pathogens including streptococci, Bacillus anthracis, and multidrug-resistant Staphylococcus pseudintermedius synthesize effector-nucleosides in order to modulate host immune cell responses.
source: In this regard, we note that many other medically highly relevant bacterial pathogens including streptococci, Bacillus anthracis, and multidrug-resistant Staphylococcus pseudintermedius synthesize effector-nucleosides in order to modulate host immune cell responses (Thammavongsa et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2017; Dai et al., 2018; Bünsow et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: (R)-DI-87-mediated inhibition of dCK may help to protect host cells from apoptotic cell death or other adverse effects during other bacterial diseases in human or animal hosts.
source: Thus, (R)-DI-87-mediated inhibition of dCK may also help to protect host cells from apoptotic cell death or other adverse effects during other bacterial diseases in human or animal hosts.
evidence: Speculation based on the mechanism of action and knowledge of other pathogens

claim: Polymicrobial infections caused by various microbial pathogens and other infectious agents that manipulate the purine salvage pathway-apoptosis axis during infection can eventually be prevented, attenuated, or treated by using (R)-DI-87.
source: Even polymicrobial infections caused by various microbial pathogens and other infectious agents that manipulate the purine salvage pathway-apoptosis axis during infection can eventually be prevented, attenuated, or treated by using (R)-DI-87.
evidence: Speculation based on the mechanism of action

claim: Administration of (R)-DI-87 did not completely abolish disease development and abscess formation during sub-lethal bloodstream infection in mice.
source: Nevertheless, administration of (R)-DI-87 did not completely abolish disease development and abscess formation during sub-lethal bloodstream infection in mice.
evidence: Observation from experimental data in Figure 4

claim: Double-pronged therapies which cover the usage of (R)-DI-87 combined with antibiotics, various anti-infective agents, or monoclonal antibodies may essentially improve disease progression during staphylococcal infections.
source: Thus, double-pronged therapies which cover the usage of (R)-DI-87 combined with antibiotics, various anti-infective agents, or monoclonal antibodies, some of which are known to neutralize predominant staphylococcal virulence determinants, including secreted toxins (Ragle and Bubeck Wardenburg, 2009; Hua et al., 2014; Thomsen et al., 2017), protein A (Kim et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2022), and specific surface antigens (Bennett et al., 2019; de Vor et al., 2022) along with usage of other host-directed therapeutics that impede S. aureus disease pathogenesis (Bravo-Santano et al., 2019; Alphonse et al., 2021), may essentially improve disease progression during staphylococcal infections.
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to published literature on combination therapies

claim: Combinatorial therapies that involve usage of (R)-DI-87 may help to enhance outcomes of life-threatening septicemia or other fatal bacterial infectious diseases.
source: Ultimately, combinatorial therapies that involve usage of (R)-DI-87 may even help to enhance outcomes of life-threatening septicemia or other fatal bacterial infectious diseases and should therefore be considered for pre-clinical tests in animal models.
evidence: Speculation about future applications

claim: (R)-DI-87-mediated inhibition of dCK is a novel host-directed therapeutic concept to mitigate staphylococcal abscess formation in organ tissues upon bloodstream infection.
source: Overall, (R)-DI-87-mediated inhibition of dCK is a novel host-directed therapeutic concept to mitigate staphylococcal abscess formation in organ tissues upon bloodstream infection.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on all experimental data presented

claim: (R)-DI-87 is extremely well tolerated in humans and currently being investigated in phase I clinical trials for the treatment of non-communicable diseases, including cancer and multiple sclerosis.
source: Since (R)-DI-87 is extremely well tolerated in humans (Kenneth A. Schultz, Trethera Corporation, Los Angeles, CA, USA; personal communication, 2023) and currently being investigated in phase I clinical trials for the treatment of non-communicable diseases, including cancer and multiple sclerosis (Poddar et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2023), this compound already meets the requirements for a prompt launch of clinical studies in individuals that suffer from local or invasive staphylococcal infections.
evidence: Supported by personal communication and citations to published literature

claim: Optimization of (R)-DI-87 or any medically acceptable derivatives thereof may aid in the design of pre-exposure prophylactic agents for hospitalized or high-risk patients.
source: Optimization of (R)-DI-87 or any medically acceptable derivatives thereof may further accelerate this process and concurrently could also aid in the design of pre-exposure prophylactic agents for hospitalized or high-risk patients, with the primary aim to enhance infection control and public health.
